analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal board that shortens drug patents and claws back tax breaks when prices are excessive.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a Patented Medicine Prices Review Board inside the FDA, staffed by people with no recent drug-industry ties. Drug makers would have to report prices and costs each year. If the board found a company charging an 'excessive price' for a patented drug, it could shorten that drug's patent term, claw back the tax breaks the company got for developing the drug, tell federal agencies not to buy the drug, and in extreme cases manufacture and sell the drug itself. Companies with a clean price record could apply to extend a patent by up to 10 percent.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who pays for prescription drugs — households, employers, insurers, and federal programs like Medicare and Medicaid — if patented-drug prices are held down. Generous price conduct could earn a modest patent extension, giving companies a reward for holding prices down.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and anyone who pays for drugs

how_it_helps.text: Each year, patent holders of prescription drugs must report to the board the prices they charge and the costs of producing and marketing each drug in the United States.

If the board finds a company charging an 'excessive price' — judged against its own price history, rival drugs in the same therapeutic class, prices charged in other countries, production costs, federal research subsidies, executive pay, and increases above inflation — it can shorten the length of the drug's patent after notice and a hearing.

The board can also require recapture of the tax benefits the company received for researching and developing the excessively priced drug, increasing the company's tax bill by the excessive portion of the price or its share of the tax benefits, whichever is smaller.
The board must report annually to every federal agency that dispenses or pays for prescription drugs, listing overpriced drugs and recommending the agency dispense a cheaper similar drug instead.
In the extreme case, the board may manufacture and sell an excessively priced drug itself, directly or by contract.

Board members must be recognized experts in consumer advocacy, medicine, pharmacology, pharmacy, or drug reimbursement, and cannot have worked in the pharmaceutical industry during the year before appointment.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name prescription drug manufacturers, who face shorter patents on overpriced drugs, clawed-back tax benefits, loss of federal-agency sales, and potential government competition with their products.

drawbacks.text: The bill works by cutting patent terms — Section 5(b) lets the board reduce a patent's length when it judges a price excessive — and shorter patents mean fewer years of exclusive sales, which weakens the financial reward for developing new drugs, the trade-off any price-control regime faces.

The 'excessive price' test rests heavily on board judgment, with the board itself deciding what increase counts as excessive under Section 5(b)(2)(B), which gives a five-member appointed board wide discretion over drug companies' core pricing decisions.

Section 5(d) authorizes the federal government to manufacture and sell a prescription drug directly, an unusually interventionist step that even supporters of drug price review might find goes further than needed.

The bill creates administrative complexity: three separate committees held jurisdiction over its pieces, and companies would face an annual reporting and hearing apparatus layered on top of the patent and tax systems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the upside is direct: patented drugs are often the most expensive part of a family's medical bills, and the bill attacks excessive prices with real levers — patent time, tax clawbacks, and federal purchasing pressure — rather than recommendations alone. The honest cost is on the other side of the ledger: the same patent exclusivity the board would trim is what funds new-drug development, and a board with discretion to judge prices 'excessive' introduces uncertainty into that system. The bill's design — reward good price conduct with modest patent extensions, punish bad conduct — tries to balance this, but the government-manufacture provision goes further than most price-regulation proposals.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced; none of them scheduled a hearing or vote, and the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on February 16, 1993, and it was referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Ways and Means Committees the same day.

In March and July 1993 it was referred to subcommittees — Health and the Environment under Energy and Commerce, and Intellectual Property and Judicial Administration under Judiciary — but no hearing or markup appears anywhere in the action history.
Stark placed more than a dozen statements about the bill in the Congressional Record between February and July 1993, the usual way a sponsor keeps a bill visible when committees are not moving it.
Thirty-five members cosponsored the bill — 34 Democrats and one Independent — and additional sponsors including Rep. Nancy Pelosi were added in February 1994, but no Republican cosponsored it.
The last action of any kind came on July 27, 1993, a year and a half before the 103rd Congress ended, and the bill never came to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers came out ahead: no board was created, so patent terms, prices, and tax benefits stayed exactly as they were, and patients and federal drug programs kept paying whatever companies charged.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were Democrats or one Independent, with no Republican support on either side of the record; the committees that let the bill sit were chaired by Democrats.

industries.note: The bill targets this industry directly: an excessively priced drug could lose patent months or years, have its tax benefits clawed back, be dropped from federal agency dispensing, and even be manufactured and sold by the government. Each mechanism cuts into the exclusive-patent revenue that supports list prices far above the cost of production.

Shortening patent terms on overpriced brand-name drugs would bring generic competition sooner, and federal agencies would be steered to substitute cheaper similar drugs — both expand the market for generics and cut costs for patients.

industries.industry: Taxpayers and federal health programs (Medicare, Medicaid, VA, NIH-funded purchasers)
industries.note: The bill requires the board to report overpriced drugs to every federal agency that pays for prescriptions and to recommend substitution, and it recaptures tax benefits given to companies that then charge excessive prices.
